content.text:
**Finding submitted: deviation (high severity).**

**What the document says**
- **§ General Provisions (c) Assignment (p0149):** blanket bar on Licensee assignment/sublicense/transfer without Licensor's prior written consent — no affiliate carve-out, no M&A successor carve-out, no reasonableness standard, and no reciprocal restriction on Licensor.
- **Article XX(a) (p0134):** any Change of Control of Licensee (asset sale, merger, or majority equity shift, per p0135) **automatically terminates the Agreement and all of our licences** unless Licensor's officer consents in advance, with Licensor "deemed reasonable" in refusing where the acquirer is competitive with Licensor or where Licensor merely "believes its interests will be adversely affected."

**Why it fails**
This is the playbook's walk-away pattern on both limbs: blanket Customer assignment prohibition with no M&A carve-out *and* a Vendor right triggered by our change of control (here, automatic termination rather than mere re-pricing). It does not reach even the fallback, which requires mutual successor assignment rights and a not-unreasonably-withheld consent standard.

**Redline (validated ok:true, preferred position)**
1. p0149 rewritten: we may assign without consent to an Affiliate (defined at 1.1) or to a successor by merger, reorganization, acquisition or sale of substantially all assets/equity; other assignments need consent not unreasonably withheld; Licensor may not assign without our consent and never to our competitor; a Change of Control is not a deemed assignment.
2. p0134(a) replaced with an express statement that a Change of Control of Licensee requires no Licensor consent and gives Licensor no termination, suspension or re-pricing right — the "CHANGE OF CONTROL" definition is preserved.

**Noted, not redlined:** Article XXII (p0139) gives Licensor a right of first refusal over our M&A transactions on a five-business-day clock, and p0137 permits termination on wind-up/dissolution. The ROFR is an exit constraint better addressed under the termination rule; I flagged it in the rationale rather than duplicating the commercial term here.
